newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court rejects child-visit appeal fee.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court rejects child-visit appeal fee.

text.p: The Supreme Court ruled Monday that states may not require that poor people pay court filing fees to bring an appeal in parental visitation cases.

The court, by a 6-3 vote, said a divorced Mississippi woman, Melissa Brooks, cannot be kept from appealing a ruling ending her visitation rights to her two children just because she could not pay more than $2,300 in court fees.
Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote for the majority that a state may not constitutionally condition appeals from trial court decrees terminating parental rights on the ability to pay the filing fees.

"Just as a state may not block an indigent petty offender's access to an appeal afforded others, so Mississippi may not deny (Brooks), because of her poverty, appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence on which the trial court found her unfit to remain a parent," she said.
Ginsburg said the high court has recognised a narrow category of civil cases in which the state must provide court access without regard to a person's ability to pay the fees.

She said the record shows appeals are few in parental visitation cases and it would not impose an "undue burden" for the state to pay for the fees. About 30 states already have taken that step for poor people.

Ginsburg said fundamental rights were at stake in the appeal, with Brooks "endeavoring to defend against the state's destruction of her family bonds and to resist the brand associated with a parental unfitness (determination)."
She said the ruling would affect only parental visitation cases, not all other civil actions, even other domestic relations matters such as divorce or paternity lawsuits.

Brooks' parental rights were terminated in 1994 after a court battle with her former husband, Sammy James, who had remarried and sought to make his new wife the children's adoptive mother. He charged Brooks had abused the children.

A trial court found Brooks was unfit. When she sought to appeal, she was told she had to pay $2,352 for a transcript of the court hearing and filing fees. She was unemployed and did not have the money.

The justices overturned a Mississippi court ruling that there was no right for poor people to proceed in civil appeals without paying the fees. Mississippi had argued that a fair trial court hearing was enough to protect parental rights.
The court's three most conservative members, Chief Justice William Rehnquist and Justices Antonin Scalia and Clarence Thomas, all dissented.

"I do not think ... that the new-found constitutional right to free transcripts in civil appeals can be effectively restricted to this case," Thomas said, warning that the ruling will result in greater demands for the states to provide free assistance to would-be appellants in all types of civil cases.
